previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, opioid dependence, and asthma was admitted for abdominal pain, shortness of breath, and hematemesis after a three-day alcohol relapse. He exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal and hepatic encephalopathy, requiring lorazepam and increased lactulose. Initial CT showed a new liver hypodensity and portal hypertension with varices; a follow-up multiphasic CT revealed regenerative nodules without HCC. EGD confirmed portal hypertensive gastropathy as the source of bleeding. He was managed with IV octreotide, ceftriaxone, and PPI, later transitioned to oral therapy. Asthma exacerbation was treated with nebulizers and inhalers. His pain improved with tramadol, and anxiety was addressed with hydroxyzine and outpatient psychiatry referral. Methadone was continued at a reduced dose. He stabilized, remained hemodynamically normal, and was discharged home with follow-up in liver and mental health clinics, advised to maintain sobriety.
problems: Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without ascites
Delirium due to known physiological condition
Other diseases of stomach and duodenum
